items.label: section_header
items.text: THE SOLUBILITY OF IONIC COMPOUNDS IN WATER THE SOLUBILITY OF IONIC COMPOUNDS IN WATER

items.label: text
items.text: To keep the table simple, it includes one or two compounds (aluminium carbonate, for example) which don't actually exist. Don't worry about these. The problem won't arise at International GCSE.

items.label: text
items.text: There is no clear line between 'insoluble' and 'almost insoluble' compounds. The ones picked out as 'almost insoluble' include the more common ones that you might need to know about elsewhere in the course.

items.label: text
items.text: It can seem a bit frightening to have to remember all this, but it isn't as difficult as it looks at first sight.

items.label: text
items.text: The reason for the exceptions in the carbonates and hydroxides is that all sodium, potassium and ammonium compounds are soluble.

items.label: text
items.text: Except for the carbonates and hydroxides, most of these compounds are soluble. Learn the exceptions in the sulfates and chlorides.

items.label: text
items.text: In the next sections we will learn about some practical methods to make salts. Before we can do this, we need to know which substances are soluble and which are insoluble in water because the method we use depends on this.

items.label: list_item
items.text: all sodium, potassium and ammonium compounds are soluble

items.label: list_item
items.text: most common chlorides are soluble, except lead(ll) chloride and silver chloride

items.label: list_item
items.text: most common sulfates are soluble, except lead(ll) sulfate, barium sulfate, silver sulfate and calcium sulfate

items.label: list_item
items.text: most common carbonates are insoluble, except sodium, potassium and ammonium carbonates

items.label: list_item
items.text: most metal hydroxides are insoluble (or almost insoluble), except sodium, potassium and ammonium hydroxides. Calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble in water.
